records.sourceFile: Association between magnetic resonance imaging use and recovery time following concussion - A CARE consortium study.pdf

paper.citation: Syrydiuk RA, Boltz AJ, Lempke LB, van Pelt K, Balendran V, Scott K, et al. Association between magnetic resonance imaging use and recovery time following concussion: a CARE consortium study. Research in Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: This study compared concussion recovery in collegiate athletes who had a research MRI within 72 hours of injury with propensity-matched athletes who did not have one. Time to return-to-play initiation and unrestricted return to play did not differ significantly after adjustment for symptom severity, although the MRI group reported higher symptom burden after injury.
paper.tldr: In a small matched sample of collegiate athletes with concussion, a research MRI was not associated with a statistically significant change in return-to-play timelines. The confidence intervals are wide, so a meaningful delay cannot be excluded.
paper.methods: Matched cohort analysis of the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium data, using the first concussion of athletes at four Advanced Research Core sites (Fall 2014 to Spring 2020). Nearest-neighbour propensity matching on sex, prior concussion, injury situation and site produced 45 MRI and 45 non-MRI athletes, and symptoms were measured with SCAT total symptom severity and BSI-18. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models estimated MRI status effects on days to return-to-play initiation and unrestricted return to play, adjusted for SCAT total symptom severity.
paper.findings: Median days to return-to-play initiation were 10 (IQR 7 to 15) with MRI and 7 (IQR 4 to 9) without (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.28 to 1.21; p = 0.23). Median days to unrestricted return were 17 (IQR 11 to 60) and 12 (IQR 8 to 24) (HR 0.77; 95% CI 0.29 to 1.26; p = 0.30). Post-injury, the MRI group had higher SCAT total symptom severity (median 38 vs 21; p = 0.01) and higher SCAT nervous/anxious ratings (p = 0.04), but BSI-18 anxiety and global severity did not differ significantly.
paper.limitations: The Table 3 confidence intervals are symmetric around the hazard ratios on the linear scale (0.75 plus or minus 0.47; 0.77 plus or minus 0.48) rather than on the log scale, which suggests they were computed on the HR scale; the exact bounds should be treated with caution. The order of MRI and symptom assessment was not recorded, so higher post-injury symptoms cannot be attributed to the scan or the injury, and post-injury scores are described as collected under 24 h in the tables but as over 24 h in the discussion. The matched sample was small (45 pairs from 2,072 eligible), 82% male and limited to NCAA high-contact sports.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff planning a research MRI after concussion can note that this matched study found no statistically significant change in return-to-play timelines, but the intervals do not exclude a large delay. The authors suggest measuring anxiety at the time of the scan in future work, since the MRI group had higher post-injury symptom scores and the study could not show whether the scan or the injury caused them.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance study. It addresses concussion recovery in collegiate athletes and does not measure training, performance or load outcomes.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return-to-play timing, but limited: it found no statistically significant difference in days to return-to-play initiation or unrestricted return between MRI and matched non-MRI athletes, with wide confidence intervals. It cannot be used to set a return-to-play criterion, to judge whether MRI findings should change clearance, or to show that MRI is clinically necessary, and the authors do not recommend mandating MRI.

records.sourceFile: Attention-deficit_hyperactivity                       disorder in elite athletes- a narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Han, D.H., McDuff, D., Thompson, D., Hitchcock, M.E., Reardon, C.L., Hainline, B. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in elite athletes: a narrative review. Br J Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of ADHD in elite athletes covering symptoms, comorbidities, effects on performance and management. The authors estimate ADHD prevalence in student and elite athletes at about 7% to 8%. They conclude that psychosocial treatment should form the foundation of management, with medication used when needed, and that prescribers must manage cardiovascular, heat and anti-doping issues.
paper.tldr: ADHD may be more common in elite athletes than in the general population, but the evidence is narrative and mostly from non-athlete samples. The authors recommend psychosocial treatment as the base of care, with careful medication management and anti-doping compliance where stimulants are used.
paper.methods: Narrative review. One author searched PubMed, SportDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus and Cochrane in November 2018, combined ADHD, sport participation and elite-level terms, and checked reference lists. Other literature was used where athlete-specific evidence was missing. Elite athletes were defined as professional, Olympic or collegiate competitors.
paper.findings: The authors estimate ADHD prevalence in student and elite athletes at about 7% to 8%, and report that 101 Major League Baseball players (about 8.4%) received therapeutic use exemptions for ADHD stimulants in the 2017 to 2018 cycle, which they note probably underestimates true prevalence. They describe possible performance effects in both directions, including impulsivity and hyperfocus that may help some athletes and attention, emotional and comorbidity problems that may impair performance. They report that stimulant side effects, including heat intolerance and cardiac risk, need monitoring in athletes, and that psychosocial interventions are recommended with or without medication.
paper.limitations: The review does not use a systematic method or a formal appraisal of study quality, and the sources are mostly general-population, child or non-athlete studies. The authors state that positive effects of ADHD on athletic performance have not been systematically studied. The link between ADHD and prolonged concussion recovery is cited to other reviews and was not assessed by the authors.
paper.practicalImplications: Team physicians, athletic trainers and prescribers should coordinate when an athlete with ADHD takes stimulant medication, including blood pressure, hydration and heat monitoring. Staff should check the athlete's anti-doping status, since stimulants require a therapeutic use exemption where prescribed. Psychosocial support can be considered alongside or instead of medication, as the authors recommend.
paper.athleteDev: The review notes that ADHD traits may help some athletes, for example through impulsivity or hyperfocus, while attention and emotional problems may hinder others. The authors state that these performance effects have not been systematically studied, so the review cannot guide training design or talent selection.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport after injury. It may inform medication safety checks, such as heat and cardiovascular risk for an athlete taking stimulants, but it does not provide evidence on concussion recovery or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Baseline Concussion Clinical Measures Are Related to Sensory Organization and Balance.pdf

paper.citation: Vander Vegt CB, Register-Mihalik JK, Ford CB, Rodrigo CJ, Guskiewicz KM, Mihalik JP. Baseline Concussion Clinical Measures Are Related to Sensory Organization and Balance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2019;51(2):264-270.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional analysis of baseline concussion assessments in 207 NCAA Division I varsity athletes tested whether symptom severity, concussion history, sex and CNS Vital Signs neurocognitive domains were associated with Sensory Organization Test (SOT) balance scores. Reaction time and executive function were associated with the composite and vestibular ratio scores, and reaction time was associated with the visual ratio score. Symptom severity, concussion history and sex were not significant contributors.
paper.tldr: At baseline, athletes with faster reaction times and better executive function had better SOT balance, but these cognitive measures explained only a modest share of balance differences. Symptom severity, concussion history and sex did not add to the models.
paper.methods: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of pre-season baseline symptom checklists, CNS Vital Signs and SOT results from varsity athletes at one NCAA Division I institution, 2014 to 2016. Symptom severity was split at the 75th percentile (high group at a score of 5 or more). Stepwise linear regression models entered sex and concussion history first, then symptom level and the CNS Vital Signs domains representing processing speed, attention and memory, with Bonferroni alpha set at 0.017.
paper.findings: After sex, concussion history and symptom level were entered, reaction time added 11% of the variance in the composite score and executive function added a further 6% (final model R2 = 0.18). Reaction time and executive function were both significant in the vestibular model (R2 = 0.14). Reaction time alone was significantly associated with the visual ratio (R2 = 0.09; final model R2 = 0.10), and no predictor was significant for the somatosensory ratio. Sex, concussion history and symptom level were not significant in any model.
paper.limitations: The design is cross-sectional and uses baseline data only, so the findings do not show how these relationships change after concussion or predict injury. The sample came from one university, was mostly male and mostly played contact or collision sports, and the authors state that clinical application may be limited by the small explained variance.
paper.practicalImplications: Baseline reaction time and executive function from CNS Vital Signs can be reviewed alongside SOT balance results when building an athlete's baseline profile. The associations are modest and cross-sectional, so they should not be used alone to label an athlete as impaired or to make a training or return-to-play decision.
paper.athleteDev: Reaction time and executive function explain part of the balance differences between athletes, so cognitive and balance measures can be reviewed together. The authors point to balance work that challenges sensory input, such as visual occlusion, perturbations, unstable surfaces and single leg stance, but the study did not test any training intervention.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-play decisions. It examined baseline measures only, and the authors state that post-injury inferences are limited, so it does not show that balance or cognitive scores change after concussion or predict re-injury.

records.sourceFile: Bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes- a narrative review.pdf

paper.citation: Currie A, Gorczynski P, Rice SM, Purcell R, McAllister-Williams RH, Hitchcock ME, et al. Bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes: a narrative review. Br J Sports Med. 2019;0:1-9.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes, including diagnosis, prevalence, impact on performance and management. The authors found little athlete-specific research, and they report that recommendations depend mainly on expert opinion and extrapolation from general population guidance.
paper.tldr: Bipolar and psychotic disorders in elite athletes are under-studied, and training, exercise and substance use can mask or mimic symptoms. Medication choice relies on expert opinion, with side effects such as sedation, weight gain and QTc prolongation weighed against sporting demands.
paper.methods: Narrative review. One author searched PubMed, SportDiscus, PsycINFO, Scopus and Cochrane (repeated in November 2018) for studies conducted only in current elite athletes that reported bipolar or psychotic disorders. Of 420 potential references, 12 met the criteria, and related references were added. Elite athletes were defined as competing at professional, Olympic or collegiate/university level.
paper.findings: No reliable prevalence data exist for bipolar or psychotic disorders in elite athletes, and schizophrenia appears under-represented. Exercise can mask or normalise overactivity in mania, and anabolic steroid and stimulant use can cause or confuse hypomanic or psychotic symptoms. Case reports indicate that high-profile athletes with bipolar disorder can still succeed, and the authors note a possible role for continued recreational exercise. Lithium needs careful monitoring, since sweat loss can lower levels and dehydration can raise them.
paper.limitations: The review rests on 12 eligible references, none of them athlete-specific trials, and the authors state that recommendations are largely expert opinion extrapolated from general population guidance. Performance effects are described from case reports and small studies, and no sports-specific psychosis screening tool exists; the 16-item Prodromal Questionnaire is a general tool that the authors suggest may help.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider a mood or psychotic disorder when an athlete shows marked changes in sleep, energy, mood or training behaviour, and do not assume extra training is only commitment, since overactivity can be hidden by training. Ask about anabolic steroid and stimulant use, and refer suspected first-episode psychosis to a specialist mental health service promptly. Medication decisions need specialist input that weighs sedation, weight gain, QTc prolongation and lithium monitoring against the athlete's sport.
paper.athleteDev: Training can hide or normalise the overactivity of mania, and the authors note vigorous exercise may precipitate or perpetuate mania, so an athlete with bipolar disorder may be limited in how much they can safely train. The authors suggest continued recreational exercise can help, and where symptoms impair elite participation, a supported exit to a lower level of sport.
paper.rtp: The review does not study return to sport after a bipolar or psychotic episode. It suggests a supported step down to lower-level sport when symptoms impair elite participation, and notes that some medications (such as aripiprazole with akathisia, or sedating agents) could affect motor function, so return decisions should rest on specialist mental health assessment.

records.sourceFile: Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Neuropathologic Change Is Not Associated With Suicide in Former Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Iverson GL. Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Neuropathologic Change Is Not Associated With Suicide in Former Athletes. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2025;35:e70086.
paper.abstract: This review responds to a 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis that concluded suicide is a potential outcome of CTE neuropathologic change, and it re-examines the four postmortem studies that assessed suicide as a manner of death. The author argues that these studies, together with other postmortem and cohort studies, show no consistent association between CTE neuropathologic change and suicide. The author concludes that the best available evidence suggests CTE neuropathologic change is not associated with depression, suicidality or suicide.
paper.tldr: A narrative critique argues that available postmortem and cohort studies show no link between CTE neuropathologic change and suicide in former athletes. The cited samples are small brain-donor series with mixed results, so the conclusion is a reading of limited evidence.
paper.methods: Narrative review that re-examines the four postmortem studies used by a 2025 meta-analysis, adds other postmortem and cohort studies, and summarizes suicide outcomes in a comparison table. It is not a systematic search, and conclusions are drawn from the reported counts and percentages.
paper.findings: The author reports that the largest included study (Daneshvar, 631 football-playing donors) found suicide less often in donors with CTE-NC (13.7% vs 26.3%, P<0.001), that McKee (2023, 152 donors under 30) found no difference (52.4% vs 60.7%), and that two small series (Suter, Taskina) showed higher rates with CTE-NC. Across the eight postmortem comparisons in Table 1, the CTE-NC group had a higher suicide rate in three, a lower rate in four and an equal rate in one; in a 336-donor study suicidality during life was 29.5% with and 33.7% without CTE-NC. The author reports that five cohort studies of former professional football or soccer players found lower or no different suicide risk than general-population men.
paper.limitations: This is a single-author narrative critique without a systematic search, and the author discloses forensic consulting on mild TBI and suicide and NFL research funding. Some numbers do not reconcile: the Iverson (2023) row of Table 1 lists 10 CTE-NC cases although the text says that study had no definitive CTE-NC and these 10 had only 'features', the Bieniek row likewise pools CTE-NC with features, and the reported odds ratio for Daneshvar (0.64, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.71) does not match the raw counts. Brain-donor series cannot estimate risk in living athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: When athletes raise concern about CTE and suicide, the author advises conveying the Concussion in Sport Group position that it is not known whether CTE-NC causes specific psychiatric problems, and instilling hope that depression and suicidality improve with treatment. The reviewed evidence does not support presenting suicide as a known outcome of CTE-NC.
paper.athleteDev: No direct performance application: the review concerns mental health and neuropathology in former athletes, not training or performance.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport, since the review does not study concussion recovery or return to play. Its relevance is to former athletes with repeated head impacts who raise concern about CTE, where the author advises conveying the knowledge gap rather than a firm answer.

records.sourceFile: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy research viewed in the public domain - What makes headlines.pdf

paper.citation: Wolfson DI, Kuhn AW, Kerr ZY, Brett BL, Yengo-Kahn AM, Solomon GS, et al. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy research viewed in the public domain: What makes headlines? Brain Injury. 2020;34(4):528-534.
paper.abstract: This systematic PubMed review identified 270 CTE-in-sport publications and coded their impact factor, publication type, football discussion and conclusion. Most publications (60%) had no primary data collection. Higher Altmetric scores were linked to primary data, CTE in the title, football discussion and, among papers concluding a contact sport-CTE association, higher impact factor.
paper.tldr: Most CTE-in-sport papers are reviews or commentaries rather than new data, and papers that link contact sport to CTE drew more online attention. Use this to understand how CTE evidence is publicized, not as evidence of CTE risk.
paper.methods: PubMed was searched on 15 October 2018 for CTE with sport terms in the title or abstract, with no exclusions. Four authors coded publication year, impact factor, data type, sample size, CTE in title, football mention and conclusion, and Altmetric scores were collected. Analyses used Wilcoxon, chi-square and multivariable ordinal logistic regression.
paper.findings: Of 270 publications, 60% had no primary data collection and 67% discussed American football; of the 268 with coded conclusions, 39% concluded a contact sport-CTE association. The median Altmetric score was 12 (range 0 to 3745). Adjusted odds ratios for a higher Altmetric level were 2.29 for primary data (95% CI 1.35 to 3.89), 2.35 for CTE in the title (1.41 to 3.92), 2.11 for football discussion (1.24 to 3.59) and, only among association-concluding papers, 2.11 per 3-point JIF increase (1.24 to 3.59).
paper.limitations: Only PubMed was searched, the paper measures attention rather than scientific quality, Altmetric scores rise over time, and the authors note that coding of football mention and conclusion involved judgment. The football and JIF odds ratios are printed identically (2.11, 1.24 to 3.59) in the abstract, results and Table 2, which may be a reporting error. The text gives 19% no association and 41% neutral, but the Table 1 footnote lists 110 no-association and 51 neutral papers, the reverse.
paper.practicalImplications: Before relying on a CTE headline, check whether the paper collects primary data or is a review or commentary. Public attention in this literature tracks positive findings and is not a measure of evidence strength.
paper.athleteDev: This paper does not measure athlete performance or training outcomes. Its relevance to performance staff is limited to understanding how CTE claims reach athletes and coaches in the media.
paper.rtp: This paper cannot inform return to sport decisions because it contains no athlete recovery, concussion or symptom data. It is relevant only to how staff weigh CTE media claims when discussing long-term brain health.
